analysis.one_liner: Requires telecom and cable networks to set aside up to a fifth of their capacity, free, for schools, libraries, governments, and nonprofits.
analysis.headline: Introduced by one senator with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee after a single subcommittee hearing and never came to a vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the FCC to make owners of telephone, cable, and other telecommunications networks reserve up to 20% of their network capacity for free public use by schools, libraries, state and local governments, public broadcasters, and nonprofits. The reserved capacity had to match the best quality the network offers, and the network owner could not control or be liable for what was said on it. It also created a public fund, paid into by the network companies, to help schools, libraries, and community groups actually use that capacity. The bill was a response to the mid-1990s buildout of the 'information superhighway,' reflecting concern that private network owners would become gatekeepers who priced out rural residents, low-income people, and nonprofit voices.
analysis.who_benefits: Schools, public and nonprofit libraries, state, local, and tribal governments, public broadcasters, and nonprofits would get free access to top-quality capacity on the nation's telecommunications networks, plus grants from a new public fund to use it. The public would gain noncommercial educational, civic, and cultural services and a wider diversity of voices on networks that the bill's own findings said would otherwise be controlled by private gatekeepers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Schools, libraries, local governments, and nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to require network owners to reserve capacity — presumed at 20% of the network — for free use by eligible public entities, with the reserved capacity treated as public property.
Requires that the reserved public capacity be equal in quality to the best capacity the network offers, including channel positioning and interconnection rights.
Creates a Public Telecommunications Infrastructure Fund financed by contributions from network owners to give schools, libraries, and community groups the money to put the reserved capacity to work.

The bill's findings state that without intervention, private carriers would exclude those with the fewest resources — rural residents, low-income people, minorities, people with disabilities, the elderly, and nonprofits — and that broad access to a diversity of voices furthers democratic self-governance.

analysis.who_pays: Telephone, cable, and other network operators would surrender up to 20% of their capacity free of charge, lose control over that capacity's content, and contribute to the new public fund. Those costs would likely show up in rates paid by subscribers or in slower network investment.

drawbacks.text: Network operators would have to give up as much as a fifth of their capacity at no charge and pay into a public fund on top of it, costs that a private company would typically recover from its paying subscribers through higher rates.

Requiring free capacity from newly built networks could reduce the incentive to invest in building them in the first place, a serious objection at a moment when carriers were deciding how much of the 'information superhighway' to construct.

The FCC could reduce or entirely eliminate a network's obligation if it found the network had open architecture and nondiscriminatory access terms, a built-in escape valve that could have hollowed out the mandate in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promised real public benefits — free, high-quality capacity for schools, libraries, and civic groups, and a funded way to use it — at a cost borne by a concentrated set of network companies and, indirectly, their subscribers. The design had weaknesses: a 20% reservation was a blunt instrument, the fund's financing was left largely to FCC rulemaking, and the FCC's power to waive the obligation could have gutted it. Whether the public benefit outweighed the cost to network investment was the central honest dispute, and the bill never got far enough for that argument to be tested in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, its communications subcommittee held one hearing, and then it sat with no committee vote and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Daniel Inouye introduced the bill on June 15, 1994, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The Subcommittee on Communications held hearings on the bill on June 22, 1994, printed as S.Hrg. 103-783.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee never reported the bill, and it never received a vote in the Senate; the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telephone and cable network operators came out ahead: they never had to give up network capacity for free public use or pay into the public fund, and the costs and obligations the bill would have imposed on them simply disappeared when the Congress ended.

for.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-HI); sponsor and chairman of the Communications Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and convened a subcommittee hearing on it nine days later.

against.name: Senate Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Ernest Hollings (D-SC)
against.what_they_did: Held one subcommittee hearing but never scheduled a markup or reported the bill to the floor.

against.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chairman, allowed the bill to die in committee without a committee vote or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Telephone, cable, and other telecommunications network operators
industries.note: The bill would have required them to reserve up to 20% of network capacity free of charge, with no control over its content, and to contribute to a public fund — a direct transfer of network capacity and money to public uses. Their cost would have been the public's gain in access.

industries.industry: Schools, libraries, public broadcasters, and nonprofits
industries.note: These would-be beneficiaries would have received free access to the best capacity on the networks plus grant money to use it. The bill's findings framed them as the voices private carriers were most likely to exclude.
